source: Knoblich, Ohlsson, Haider & Rhenius (1999) Constraint relaxation and chunk decomposition in insight problem solving
finding: Founding statement of representational change theory (RCT). An impasse arises when the active constraints and perceptual chunks leave no solution in the search space. It is broken by relaxing a constraint or decomposing a chunk. Both processes are specified so they predict the difficulty order of individual problems.
numbers: Four experiments with matchstick arithmetic (Roman numerals, move one stick): Exp 1A N=20, Exp 1B N=38, Exp 2 N=78, Exp 3 N=34. 5-min limit per problem.
quote: The authors hypothesized that impasses are broken by changing the problem representation
limits: Tested on one task family only (single-move Roman numeral equations). Which constraints and chunks are active is the authors' assumption, not measured.
agent_relevance: O4 (drop a constraint) and O6 (change representation) get a named mechanism: a failing output is explained by a wrongly active constraint or chunk, not by lack of search.

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson, Haider & Rhenius (1999) Constraint relaxation and chunk decomposition in insight problem solving
finding: Constraint relaxation is ordered by scope. Three constraints map to three levels: value constraint (numerals), operator constraint (functional terms), tautology constraint (whole equation). The higher the level, the lower the chance it is relaxed. Predicted ease: Type A (change a value) > Type B (change an operator) > Type C (tautology X = X).
numbers: Prediction: solution frequency A > B > C; solution time A < B < C on first encounter.
limits: Scope ranking is stipulated from the authors' analysis of arithmetic, not from an independent scale. The authors state they had no interval scale, so they could not order Type D against B and C.
agent_relevance: Gives a ranking rule for which assumption to drop first when O4 fires: drop narrow-scope assumptions before wide-scope ones.

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson, Haider & Rhenius (1999) Constraint relaxation and chunk decomposition in insight problem solving
finding: Chunk decomposition is ordered by tightness. A chunk whose parts are themselves chunks is loose (VII = V + I + I). A chunk whose parts are not meaningful chunks is tight (V, X, I, minus sign). Loose chunks are decomposed first; tight ones only if failure persists. Plus and equal signs are classed as intermediate. Type D problems (break a tight chunk, e.g. X into two slanted sticks) should be harder than Type A.
numbers: Hypothesis 2: Type D solved less often and slower than Type A on Block 1.
limits: Chunk classification is by the authors' judgment. Authors say chunk decomposition is not under conscious control, which makes it hard to induce on purpose.
agent_relevance: O6 for an LLM means re-parsing the input into finer parts (characters, digits, sub-expressions) when the whole-unit parse fails.

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson, Haider & Rhenius (1999) Constraint relaxation and chunk decomposition in insight problem solving
finding: Transfer hypothesis: once a constraint is relaxed or a chunk decomposed, it stays so, and initial difficulty differences disappear on the second block. Harder types should show larger transfer.
numbers: Exp 1A (N=20): problem type F(3,57)=7.11, p<.001; block F(1,19)=14.41; type x block F(3,57)=3.24, p<.05. Type B and C improved (p<.05, p<.001), Type A did not (p=.80). Type D 75% to 90% (p=.13).
limits: Several transfer tests were non-significant, which the authors blame on ceiling effects (75% already solved in Block 1 for D).
agent_relevance: A representation change learned on one item should carry to similar items. A note of which constraint was dropped could be reused across a problem class.

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson, Haider & Rhenius (1999) Constraint relaxation and chunk decomposition in insight problem solving
finding: Exp 2 (N=78) replicated the difficulty order with a larger sample of American students. Similarity between Block 1 and Block 2 problems did not matter, so transfer is about the representation change, not surface match.
numbers: Block 1 solved 66% overall, Block 2 96%. Type effect F(4,222)=46.45, p<.001. Similarity effect F(3,74)=0.34 (n.s.). Block 1 by similarity condition: 67%, 64%, 64%, 71%. Type A vs B not significant (p=.14), B < C p<.001, D < A p<.001.
limits: A vs B difference was not significant in frequency in Exp 1B (p=.12) or Exp 2 (p=.14); only in solution time. Ceiling: more than 75% of Type B solved.
agent_relevance: Supports carrying a dropped constraint across items regardless of surface similarity.

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson, Haider & Rhenius (1999) Constraint relaxation and chunk decomposition in insight problem solving
finding: Exp 3 (N=34) separated the two sources of difficulty. Showing the tautological form (X = X) removes the difficulty of Type C but leaves Type D (chunk) untouched. Prior exposure to tautology problems helped regular Type C problems.
numbers: Regular Type C solved 61% in Block 1 (regular-first group); tautological Type C 100%. Type D: 61% regular-first vs 69% tautology-first (chi2(1,N=34)=0.22, p=.64); Block 2 92% vs 94%. Type A 94% and 97%.
limits: Unexpected result: tautological Type A problems took longer than regular ones. Authors give an ad hoc explanation (solvers first tried to keep the regular form).
agent_relevance: Strong evidence that showing that a normally forbidden form is allowed removes the barrier. An explicit 'is this form allowed?' check is a cheap O4 candidate.

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson, Haider & Rhenius (1999) Constraint relaxation and chunk decomposition in insight problem solving
finding: Solution time order matched frequency. Type A solved faster than B, B faster than C, A faster than D, in the experiments that tested it.
numbers: Exp 1A (N=20): A<B T=12 p<.001; B<C T=41 p<.05; A<D T=10 p<.001. Exp 1B (N=38): A<B T=107 p<.001; B<C T=160 p<.01; A<D T=96 p<.001. Block 2 medians in Exp 1A: A 33 s, B 38 s, C 10 s, D 42 s.
limits: Times for unsolved problems were set to the 5-min cap, so times are conservative. Skewed data analysed with ordinal tests.
agent_relevance: Time to find the right move is a measurable signature. Our harness can log attempts-to-fix by operator class.

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson, Haider & Rhenius (1999) Constraint relaxation and chunk decomposition in insight problem solving
finding: Competing explanations were weighed. Gestalt reorganization is too vague to predict individual problem differences. Blind variation and selection cannot predict move order or differential transfer. Functional fixedness explains why impasses arise but not how they end. Mental ruts predicts recovery only after a pause. Gradual transformation of experience is implausible for matchstick arithmetic.
numbers: Tables 13 and 14 summarise: the predicted order of difficulty was never violated across Exp 1A, 1B, 2 (non-significant cases attributed to ceiling).
limits: The paper argues by elimination and fit, not by a head-to-head quantitative model comparison. Later work (Ormerod & MacGregor 2020) offers a rival account.
agent_relevance: Defines what RCT adds over generic 'try again': it says which parts of the representation to change, and in what order.

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson & Raney (2001) An eye movement study of insight problem solving
finding: Eye movements fit three RCT predictions: longer fixations as impasse sets in; early attention biased to values (not operators); and a late shift of attention to the crucial element only in solvers. Rival impasse theories predict the first only.
numbers: N=24, three problems, 5-min limit. Solved: Problem A (change result value) 23/24; B (change operator) 9/24; C (tight chunk X) 18/24. A vs B chi2(1)=18.38, p<.001; A vs C chi2=4.18, p<.05; B vs C chi2=4.78, p<.05.
limits: Small sample; only three problems. Eye data are correlational.
agent_relevance: Attention allocation may be a measurable signal: which parts of the prompt the reasoning revisits could flag a stuck representation.

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson & Raney (2001) An eye movement study of insight problem solving
finding: Initial attention is biased to values. Long fixations went more to the result and operands than to plus and equal signs, as if operators were treated as constants. Short fixations showed no such bias.
numbers: Long fixations, element effect F(3,63)=24.02, p<.001; no effect of problem (p=.42). Short fixations element effect F(3,63)=2.82, p<.05. Plus and equal signs got clearly less than the chance level of 20% of fixation time.
limits: Chance level of 20% per element is the authors' baseline across five elements.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that the default representation hides operators. The agent could list the 'fixed' parts of a problem explicitly so they can be questioned.

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson & Raney (2001) An eye movement study of insight problem solving
finding: At the moment of insight attention moves to the part that must change, but only in solvers. In Problem B successful solvers increased long-fixation time on the operators across three intervals; unsuccessful solvers did not. In Problem C, successful solvers looked at the result (the tight chunk) much more in the final interval.
numbers: Problem B long fixations: success x interval F(1,22)=7.91, p<.01; early short-fixation difference F(1,22)=7.09, p<.05. Problem C long fixations: interval F(2,42)=5.31, p<.01; success x interval F(2,42)=5.08, p<.05.
limits: Intervals are thirds of each person's own solving time. Main effect of success not significant in several tests.
agent_relevance: Suggests insight is preceded by a targeted look at the previously ignored element, which O4 should force by naming it.

source: Ormerod & MacGregor (2020) The complementary roles of knowledge and strategy in insight problem-solving (CogSci 42)
finding: Partial replication with a rival account. Tight-chunk problems were harder than loose-chunk ones (RCT confirmed), but a large value disparity in the equation nearly erased the chunk effect. The authors argue that progress monitoring (look for moves that reduce the gap) explains solution without relaxing anything.
numbers: Exp 1 (N=121 after exclusions): low-value loose 77% (23/30), low-value tight 43% (13/30), high-value loose 90% (28/31), high-value tight 77% (24/31). Logistic model chi2(3,N=121)=21.6, p=.001.
limits: Matchstick algebra, not arithmetic. Paper booklet task run in groups. Value manipulation confounds chunk difficulty with cue strength.
agent_relevance: Warns that cues to progress can matter as much as constraint drops. O4 should be paired with a progress signal and tested against it.

source: Ormerod & MacGregor (2020) The complementary roles of knowledge and strategy in insight problem-solving (CogSci 42)
finding: Scope effect (tautology constraint) replicated: standard tautology problems were harder than reverse tautologies, where the form is already given. High numeric disparity again removed most of the difficulty.
numbers: Exp 2 (N=133): standard tautology low-value 12% (4/32), high-value 62% (21/34); reverse tautology low 72% (23/32), high 77% (28/35). Logistic chi2(3,N=133)=39.30, p<.001; tautology Wald=19.33; value Wald=11.12; interaction Wald=5.26, p=.022.
quote: the mind's 'response to persistent failure' is not to try to forget what it knows; it is to try to find something better.
limits: Authors conclude constraint relaxation is unnecessary to explain solving; this is their interpretation, with no implemented model. Ohlsson (2011) is said to give only a partial specification.
agent_relevance: The 12% vs 62% swing from a surface cue shows that cheap cues can look like insight. Our evaluation should control for such cues.

source: Kershaw & Ohlsson (2001) Training for insight: the case of the nine-dot problem (CogSci)
finding: RCT-style analysis of the nine-dot problem. Three hypothesised sources of difficulty (perceptual, knowledge, process). Training that removed the perceptual barrier (turn on a non-dot point) raised solving, and training that reinforced the barrier lowered it.
numbers: N=90 (30 per group). First insight problem solved: facilitating training 63% (19/30), hindering 27% (8/30), no training 37% (11/30). Chi2(2,N=90)=8.836, p<.05. Among facilitating-group people who completed training, 89% (17/19) solved vs 18% (2/11) of those who did not. Baseline for undergraduates quoted as under 5%.
limits: Conference paper; one problem. The control group rate (37%) is far above the quoted under-5% baseline, so sample or instructions differ from older studies.
agent_relevance: Priming with examples in context can lower or raise insight success. Few-shot examples could hurt as much as help (mental set).

source: Kershaw & Ohlsson (2004) Multiple causes of difficulty in insight: the case of the nine-dot problem
finding: Reports three experiments saying difficulty has several interacting causes (perception, knowledge, process), and no single factor accounts for it.
numbers: Numbers not obtained (only abstract-level text was seen via search).
limits: Not opened. Treat as a pointer.
agent_relevance: Do not expect one operator to fix every impasse; a mix of reframes may be needed.

source: Oellinger, Jones & Knoblich (2006) Heuristics and representational change in two-move matchstick arithmetic tasks
finding: Extends RCT to two-move problems. Degree of representational change required strongly predicted solution rates. The effectiveness of heuristics had minimal effect. Authors give a model in which representational change is the precondition for heuristics to work on the right representation.
numbers: N=120. Per-condition percentages not obtained (full text blocked; abstract only).
limits: Not opened. Heuristic-vs-restructuring is a competing story; this paper comes down for restructuring.
agent_relevance: Order matters: restructure first, then search. Supports a state graph where reframing precedes search.

source: Jones (2003) Testing two cognitive theories of insight (JEP:LMC 29, 1017-1027)
finding: Tests RCT and progress monitoring theory in an unlimited-move problem using eye movements. The abstract returned by search was cut off, so which theory it favoured is unknown to us.
numbers: Not obtained.
limits: Not opened. Cannot say which theory won.
agent_relevance: Pointer for Angle B/C agents.

source: Oellinger, Jones, Faber & Knoblich (2013) Cognitive mechanisms of insight: heuristics and representational change in the eight-coin problem
finding: Six new versions of the eight-coin problem. Two sources of difficulty: assuming a 2D solution space, and breaking perceptual groupings. Move choices followed the current representation more than heuristics.
numbers: Numbers not obtained (abstract-level only).
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Another domain where grouping and a hidden 2D assumption block solutions: consistent with a 'hidden assumption' operator.

source: Ohlsson (1992) Information-processing explanations of insight and related phenomena (Advances in the Psychology of Thinking, Vol 1, 1-44)
finding: Origin of the theory: insight as impasse, then change of the problem representation, then new search. Known here only through the 1999 paper's description and citations; the chapter and the 2011 book were not found online.
numbers: None obtained directly. The 1999 paper credits Ohlsson 1992 for the constraint idea and Ohlsson 1990 for chunk decomposition.
limits: Not opened. Later agents should obtain the book text.
agent_relevance: Source for the three-way mechanism list.

source: Haq, Chhaya, Pandey & Bhattacharya (2025) Is your LLM trapped in a Mental Set? (arXiv 2501.11833)
finding: Adapts a human mental-set task (math equivalence, DeCaro 2016) to Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.1-70B and GPT-4o. In-context examples raised exact-match accuracy but did not change the number of steps. Zero-shot chain-of-thought made models use more steps, which the authors read as a mental-set effect.
numbers: Only six problems per condition. Few-shot only (Table 1): GPT-4o EM 0.33, 0.66, 0.66, 0.83 across the four conditions; Llama-70B 0, 0.16, 0, 0.66. With few-shot + CoT (Table 2) GPT-4o 0.66, 0.66, 0.83, 0.83; steps 3 in all cells.
limits: Tiny sample, no statistics. Mental set is not the same as representational change. Treat as an anecdote.
agent_relevance: Warns that chain-of-thought can lock in a long procedure where a shortcut exists.

source: d'Aliberti & Horta Ribeiro (2026) The Illusion of Insight in Reasoning Models (arXiv 2601.00514)
finding: Mid-trace 'Wait, let's re-evaluate' strategy shifts are rare in RL-trained reasoning models and are linked to lower accuracy. Triggering a reconsideration from outside when token entropy is high does raise accuracy.
numbers: 1M+ traces; shifts in 6.31% of traces overall; accuracy 2.57% for shifted vs 16.44% for non-shifted traces; formal 'Aha' events about 1.79% of samples under a lax detector. Domains: cryptic crosswords, math, Rush Hour puzzles; Qwen2.5 and Llama models up to 8B, plus checks on external models.
limits: Detects only lexicalised shifts; authors admit unlexicalised representational changes may be missed. Models are small and GRPO-trained.
agent_relevance: Supports G1 and O4: a rethink triggered by code on an uncertainty signal helps, while a self-initiated 'wait' does not. Use an external trigger, not the model's own aha.

source: Nasvytis & Fan (2026) Leveraging speech to identify signatures of insight and transfer in problem solving (arXiv 2605.12970)
finding: Human matchstick arithmetic (Roman numerals), five problems with think-aloud. When the same transformation type repeated, later accuracy was much higher; people spoke more at the first success and were more likely to name the problem type spontaneously. Speech was analysed with NLP (embeddings, classifiers).
numbers: N=189 online participants; 47.5% correct overall (449/945 trials). By type: value-loose-chunk 80.7% (easiest), tautological 19.2% (hardest). After first success: 83.7% correct on later problems in the Same condition vs 44.0% in the Different condition; later solve time 89.9 s vs 179.0 s (as reported).
limits: Online sample; think-aloud may change strategy. Replicates the 1999 difficulty order on a new sample. Verbal precursors before first success were hard to find.
agent_relevance: Naming the discovered problem type seems to carry the insight forward: store 'this class needs constraint X dropped' as a labelled note.

source: Nazonazo benchmark paper: The Metacognitive Bottleneck: Japanese Riddles Reveal Fundamental Limits of Machine Insight (arXiv 2509.14704)
finding: 201 Japanese children's riddles that need insight-like restructuring (framed on Knoblich 1999 and Ohlsson 1992). Most models are far below humans. Reasoning models beat non-reasoning ones. A named failure: verification failure, where the correct answer appears in the thought log and is then rejected.
numbers: Human reference on a 120-item subset, n=126: 52.9% mean. Non-reasoning models 7.6%, reasoning models 17.6%; on the full 201 items group means 9.42% vs 19.25%; odds ratio 2.29. GPT-5 inside the human 95% CI. Verification failures were 5.23% to 39.34% of wrong answers across four models (Grok 4 39.34%, Gemini 2.5 5.23%). 38 models; parameter count did not predict accuracy, release date did.
limits: Riddles are wordplay, not matchstick constraints. No operator ablation. Verification counts come from only four models with usable thought logs.
agent_relevance: Directly relevant: the agent may generate the restructured answer and then discard it. A code-side check (G3, G5) should decide, not the model's feeling.

source: MathSticks: A benchmark for visual symbolic compositional reasoning with matchstick puzzles (arXiv 2510.00483)
finding: Seven-segment matchstick equations, fix by moving one or two sticks. 1.41 million solvable instances. Vision-language models do well only when the equation text is given; in pure vision they collapse; humans exceed 90%.
numbers: 14 VLMs. With text: o3 60.00% average, Gemini-2.5-Pro 45.25%, Gemini-2.5-Flash 26.50%, o4-mini 24.75%, Seed-1.6-Thinking 21.50%, Claude Sonnet 4 2.25%, GPT-4o 0.00%. Without text: o3 38.50%, Gemini-2.5-Pro 22.50%, Seed-1.6-Thinking 1.00%, Claude Sonnet 4 0.00%. Humans 91.72%. 82.01% of items need two sticks; 4.18% one stick.
limits: Seven-segment digits, not Roman numerals, so the tight/loose chunk theory is not tested. Level 4 is 79% of the data. No RCT-based problem classes.
agent_relevance: Shows the perception step (parse into sticks) is a major bottleneck, which is the chunk-decomposition problem. Text helps, so an explicit re-encoding step (O6) should help.

source: Jiang, Ilievski, Ma & Sourati (2023) BRAINTEASER: Lateral thinking puzzles for large language models (arXiv 2310.05057, EMNLP 2023)
finding: Multiple-choice lateral-thinking puzzles (sentence and word puzzles) that require breaking default commonsense assumptions. Strong LLMs of 2023 are far below humans, and worse when the same puzzle is rephrased. Adding commonsense knowledge did not help on sentence puzzles.
numbers: About 1,100 puzzles. ChatGPT about 53% and 63% (sentence and word puzzles) against chance 25% and human about 92% (102-question expert sample). Group accuracy over original plus semantic and context reconstruction falls sharply for all models.
limits: 2023 models; later reasoning models do much better (see Nazonazo). Multiple choice allows guessing. Not matchstick, so mapping to constraint relaxation is by analogy.
agent_relevance: Key design lesson: test with rephrased variants to avoid memorised answers when asking whether an LLM drops a default assumption.

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson, Haider & Rhenius (1999) Constraint relaxation and chunk decomposition in insight problem solving
finding: Formal and computational status. RCT is stated as probabilities of relaxing or decomposing (scope and tightness orderings), with no implemented simulation in this paper. The authors say there are no models of chunk decomposition in the literature. Ormerod & MacGregor (2020) say the only specification is Ohlsson (2011), partial and based on spreading activation with inhibition.
numbers: No fitted model parameters. Predictions are rank orders over problem types only.
limits: Gap: no executable RCT model was found in any opened source. Do not assume one exists.
agent_relevance: We could build the first operational version: an ordered list of constraints by scope, tried narrowest first, with success logged per class.

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson, Haider & Rhenius (1999) Constraint relaxation and chunk decomposition in insight problem solving
finding: Backward citations. Knoblich & Haider (1996) and Knoblich & Wartenberg (1998) are cited as earlier support: matchstick arithmetic is unsolvable if arithmetic constraints are kept, and chunk decomposition needs the perceptual parse to change. The theory builds on Ohlsson (1992a, 1996) and Ohlsson & Rees (1991) for the idea that knowledge consists of constraints.
numbers: Citation chain only; those earlier papers were not opened.
limits: Backward citations are as described in the 1999 paper's text.
agent_relevance: Background for representing 'what a solution must satisfy' as explicit constraints.

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson, Haider & Rhenius (1999) Constraint relaxation and chunk decomposition in insight problem solving
finding: Boundary conditions found. Gains vanish at ceiling (Type B above 80% in Exp 2). Surface similarity of the second problem did not change transfer. Transfer is specific to the representation actually changed (tautology exposure helped Type C but not Type D in Exp 3).
numbers: Exp 3: Type D regular 61% vs tautology-first 69%, n.s. Exp 2: similarity main effect F(3,74)=0.34, n.s.
limits: No general 'insight skill' transfer was shown.
agent_relevance: A stored reframe should be tagged by the constraint it dropped, and reused only for items with the same constraint.

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson & Raney (2001) An eye movement study of insight problem solving
finding: Rival impasse principles (functional fixedness, mental ruts, Einstellung, insufficient progress) share the prediction that fixation time rises over the solving period but do not predict where attention goes at the moment of insight. This is why the authors claim RCT is better supported.
numbers: Fixation duration rose across intervals in Problems B and C but not A (Figure 3; no test statistic quoted in the text read).
limits: Follow-up (Ormerod & MacGregor 2020) shows progress monitoring can also account for solution; the contest is not settled.
agent_relevance: Keep G1 (doubt only on signal): a rising stuck-ness signal is a trigger, but the repair should target a specific element.
